source.publisher: U.S. Department of Commerce, Department of the Treasury, and Department of Justice
source.title: Tri-Seal Compliance Note: Cracking Down on Third-Party Intermediaries Used to Evade Russia-Related Sanctions and Export Controls

summary: This March 2023 U.S. tri-seal compliance note from Commerce, Treasury (OFAC) and Justice warns that malign actors continue evading Russia-related sanctions and export controls by using third-party intermediaries, front/shell companies and transshipment points to disguise SDNs, Entity List parties and Russian end users. It lists compliance red flags for financial institutions and exporters (reluctance to disclose end use, shell-company wire transfers, IP/location mismatches, transshipment routing through hubs such as China, Hong Kong, Macau, Armenia, Turkey and Uzbekistan) and summarizes OFAC/BIS designation and enforcement actions -- AO PKK Milandr's front-company procurement network, Vorago Technologies' Bulgarian-front shipment of controlled components to Russia, and sanctioned Iranian drone entities -- plus DOJ criminal indictments (the Orekhov and Grinin cases) describing tactics such as shell-company networks posing as intermediaries, divided shipments, use of aliases, underestimated invoice values, and layered fund transfers into U.S. bank accounts to obscure audit trails.

typologies.label: Name Screening Evasion

citations.quote: Using aliases for the identities of the intermediaries and end users21;

typologies.review_justification: Found in Criminal enforcement section, tactics bullet list, page 5. SAN005 doctrine: 'Name Screening Evasion is the defeat of list-based screening through the form of the name: aliases, transliterations, suffix variants... that let a listed party transact under a name an exact-match filter never flags.' The advisory alleges defendants used aliases for the intermediaries and end users in the procurement scheme -- the same mechanism of engineering the name on transaction paperwork so it will not resolve to the true (potentially listed) party during screening.

typologies.label: Third Party Payment Abuse

citations.quote: Payment coming from a third-party country or business not listed on the End-User Statement3 or other applicable end-user form;

typologies.review_justification: Found in Red flag list, page 2. TBML008 doctrine: 'Third Party Payment Abuse settles a trade through a payer who is not the trade counterparty... The payment breaks the link between the trade and the funds.' This red flag names exactly that pattern -- settlement arriving from a country or business absent from the end-user paperwork governing the underlying trade -- matching the Third-Party Payer indicator directly.

typologies.label: Rapid Movement

citations.quote: Transferring funds from shell companies in foreign jurisdictions into U.S. bank accounts and quickly forwarding or distributing funds to obfuscate the audit trail or the foreign source of the money22;

typologies.review_justification: Found in Criminal enforcement section, tactics bullet list, page 5. BA005 doctrine: Rapid Movement 'is defined by HOW FAST the funds move' -- funds land and clear back out almost immediately -- as distinct from BA008 Layering's distance/opacity axis (already claimed for this same allegation). The advisory's own word 'quickly forwarding' names the velocity element BA005 captures, over and above the multi-hop distance BA008 addresses. Single-sentence evidence limits this to low confidence.

typologies.label: Shipment Splitting to Evade Export Control Detection

citations.quote: Dividing shipments of controlled items into multiple, smaller shipments to try to avoid law enforcement detection20;

typologies.review_justification: Found in Criminal enforcement section, tactics bullet list, page 5. No library typology covers this mechanism: BA001 Structuring addresses cash deposits kept under a CTR reporting threshold (a financial-transaction pattern), and TBML003 Multiple Invoicing addresses raising several invoices against one shipment (a documentary pattern), neither of which is dividing the physical goods movement itself into smaller consignments to stay below detection thresholds. The advisory describes a distinct physical-shipment fragmentation technique for export-control evasion that the current library does not name.

extraction_notes: Five typology links proposed to the Knowledge Centre review queue (SAN003, SAN004, SAN007, BA008, TBML002U); none scored as emergent. Two red-flag tactics described on page 5 -- dividing shipments into smaller lots, and using aliases for intermediary/end-user identities -- had no typology search result above or meaningfully near the confirm floor, so they are retained only as indicators, not linked typologies. For the dual-use-goods diversion described on pages 4-5, the search tool returned both SAN007 (sanctions family) and TBML007 (tbml family) at equal top score; SAN007 was chosen because the document's overall framing is sanctions/export-control enforcement rather than trade-finance/TBML, but a reviewer weighting this for the trade desk may prefer to additionally link TBML007. The Orekhov and Grinin defendant groups are captured as category actors (nationality/role groupings) rather than named individuals because the note itself does not name the individual defendants, only case citations to sealed indictments. Page markers align 1:1 with the document's own printed page numbers throughout this 6-page note. Merged 4 reviewer addition(s) under schema 1.4.0; each carries its review_justification. Extraction-only record retained at data/records/.
